tagline.text: A surf town where waves and bonfires await on gray sand

image.credit: Iloilo Wanderer / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

items.credit: Iloilo Wanderer / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A small coastal town in San Felipe, Zambales, and one of the closest surf beaches to Manila. Gentle waves breaking over a sandy bottom make it an easy place to learn to surf, and the free-spirited scene of bonfires dotting the beach every night is a big part of the appeal.
Liwliwa is a coastal town in San Felipe, Zambales province, about
180km

northwest of Manila. Its name, said to mean "leisure" or "enjoyment" in Ilocano, once described a quiet fishing village, but from the 2010s surfers began arriving in numbers, turning it into a surf town lined with surf camps, guesthouses, and small cafés.
The sand here is gray, built up from volcanic ash that washed down the rivers after Mount Pinatubo's

eruption. The beach opens out for a long stretch toward the South China Sea, and with a sandy bottom, it gets beach-break waves with little risk of hitting rock or coral. Waves are consistent and moderate in size on most days, which is why local instructors rank it as the best spot on the west coast to learn to surf.

Liwliwa's real charm is its atmosphere. Surf shops and huts built from bamboo and palm leaves line the beach, and once the sun goes down, bonfires spring up everywhere, drawing travelers and local surfers together. Accommodation here leans toward simple, easygoing options — tents, hostels, glamping — rather than upscale resorts.

It suits anyone wanting to try surfing for the first time, and young travelers or groups of friends looking for an easy weekend getaway. That said, it's worth knowing the water isn't the turquoise of Boracay, and rain is frequent during surf season. It's also easy to pair with island hopping to Anawangin and Nagsasa Cove out of Pundaquit.
Learn with an instructor and a rented board at one of the beach's surf shops. Lessons run about
for
1 hour
, and most beginners manage to stand up on the board during their first lesson.

blocks.title: Rent a board and surf freely

children.text: If you already have experience, you can just rent a board and catch some waves. Rental runs about
per
1 hour
— aim for the morning, when the waves are gentler.
Take a seat on the beach as the sun drops into the South China Sea. After the sunset fades, every guesthouse lights a bonfire and plays music, kicking off a proper surf-town night.
About
20–30 minutes
inland by tricycle, Anghalo Falls tumbles down in three tiers into a swimming hole. Admission runs about
, a good alternative for a day with no surf.

Ride an ATV across the wide sand flats left behind when lahar (volcanic mudflow) swept through after Mount Pinatubo's eruption. Both short and guided longer routes are available, giving you a close-up look at terrain shaped by the volcano.
On calm-wave days, many people skimboard in the shallows or play beach volleyball on the sand. It's also an easy spot for kids to play by the water.

Bamboo-built cafés, taco stands, and Filipino home-style eateries are scattered along the beach. Carrying a cold drink from one beach café to the next after surfing is a classic Liwliwa way to unwind.
From Pundaquit, about
30–40 minutes
away by car, you can rent an outrigger boat and cover the Capones Island lighthouse, Camara Island, and Anawangin and Nagsasa Coves in a single day. A three-stop hopping trip runs about
per boat — be sure to ask whether life vests are included.

If you're staying an extra day, head to Pundaquit, about 30–40 minutes away by car, and add island hopping to Anawangin and Nagsasa Coves and Capones Island.
Take a bus toward Iba or Santa Cruz, Zambales from the Victory Liner terminal in Cubao, Pasay, or Caloocan, Manila, and get off at the San Felipe public market. The express via SCTEX takes about
4–5 hours
, with a one-way fare of around
, while the local bus through town takes over an hour longer but is a bit cheaper.
From the San Felipe market to Liwliwa beach is about
10–15 minutes
, around
per person if shared. Tricycles are scarce late at night, so it's best to ask your accommodation to arrange a pickup.
Take the NLEX and SCTEX, exit at Tipo, pass through Subic and Olongapo, then follow the Zambales coastal road north through San Antonio and San Narciso. It takes about
3 hours 30 minutes–4 hours 30 minutes
from Manila. Most accommodations have parking.
Coming from Korea, Clark International Airport (CRK) is the nearest option. It's about
2–3 hours
away by car, and by public transport you'll transfer to an Iba-bound bus in Olongapo.
Surf season generally runs
July–February
, with the best waves during
August–October

, when the southwest monsoon (Habagat) pushes in swell. This period is also the rainy season with frequent showers, and waves can grow large enough to be dangerous for beginners as typhoons approach, so follow your instructor's judgment. The cooler
November–February
stretch sees less rain and mostly moderate waves, making it the easiest time to combine surfing with general travel.
March–May
is clear with calm seas, good for swimming and camping, but there's almost no swell, making surfing difficult. Midday temperatures climb close to
, and accommodations fill up during summer break and Holy Week, so book ahead. On days with a typhoon warning, the coastal road and beach access may be restricted.
During Holy Week

, more than 10,000 travelers flocked to San Felipe, and about 150 accommodations on the beach were almost fully booked around Good Friday, and on Maundy Thursday several jellyfish appeared on the beach and authorities issued a swimming caution. During Holy Week and summer-vacation weekends, book accommodation weeks ahead, and check the notices posted on the beach and your accommodation's announcements before you go in the water.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Accommodation is mostly surf camps, hostels, tent campsites, and glamping sites strung along the beach. A dorm bed or tent runs about
a night, and an air-conditioned private room or glamping tent runs about

, with prices rising on weekends and during peak season. Staying at a surf camp is convenient, since lessons and board rental are handled in one place. Many buildings are bamboo with thin walls, and music can run late into the night, so if you want quiet, choose a spot a bit away from the beach's center.

The food scene is varied, as befits a surf town. Smoothie bowls and coffee at beach cafés, tacos and burgers, adobo and sinigang at Filipino home-style karinderias, and charcoal-grilled fish and squid are all popular. A karinderia meal runs about
, while cafés and restaurants run about
. Zambales is famous for its sweet mangoes, so during the
April–May
season, be sure to pick some up at the San Felipe market.
There are no ATMs on the beach. Withdraw plenty of cash from an ATM in San Felipe town before heading out.
Phone signal is weak and drops out often. Guesthouse Wi-Fi tends to be slow too, so handle any important calls in advance.
If you're a beginner, it's best to take your lesson during the calm-wind hours of
6–9 AM
. Afternoon wind often breaks up the waves.
Taking 2–3 lessons in a row with the same instructor speeds up your progress. Check whether board rental time is included in the lesson fee.
A rash guard and surf leggings protect your skin from the sun, board friction, and jellyfish.
Sand flies (nik-nik) get bad in the evening, so be sure to bring strong insect repellent.
Weekends get crowded with travelers from Manila. Go on a weekday for quieter waves, and book peak-season weekend accommodation early.

Even during surf season, some days have no waves at all. Check a surf forecast app or ask your accommodation ahead of time, and stay flexible enough to switch your plans to the waterfall or island hopping if there's no swell.
There is no public transport to Anghalo Falls, so it is common to hire a tricycle round trip from Liwliwa, at about
per tricycle including waiting time. Near the falls' entrance you can also ride a carabao cart that carries up to six people (about

The beach has no lifeguard, and rip currents form during surf season. If you're swept out, swim parallel to the beach to get free, and beginners shouldn't go in without an instructor on big-wave days.
Large waves that roll in as a typhoon approaches are dangerous even for experienced surfers. Follow PAGASA forecasts and local instructors' judgment.
Don't drop in on a wave another surfer is already riding — it can cause a collision and friction with local surfers.
The sand gets very hot at midday and UV exposure is strong. Pay attention to staying hydrated and protected from the sun.
Heavy drinking around the bonfire and swimming at night are common causes of accidents. Stay out of the water after dark.
Don't leave valuables unattended in beach huts or tents.
The Liwliwa coast is heavily eroded, and since around
July 2025
waves have swept away huts and buildings built close to the beach, and in
August–September 2026

part of the seawall and a temporary rock embankment collapsed, directly damaging nine resorts and forcing several to close temporarily. If you go in the rainy season, check ahead that your booked accommodation is operating and what condition the beach is in.
